analysis.one_liner: Caps damages in medical malpractice and medical product lawsuits and limits lawyers' fees, overriding state laws.
analysis.headline: The bill caps pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000, restricts attorney fees, and shields FDA-approved drug and device makers from punitive damages — but never received a vote, dying in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The HEALTH Act would rewrite the rules for nearly every lawsuit over medical care, drugs, and devices nationwide. It caps compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury, caps lawyers' contingency fees, shortens the deadlines for filing a claim, makes it far harder to win punitive damages, and blocks punitive damages entirely against makers of FDA-approved drugs and devices. It would also override state laws that give injured patients stronger protections. The bill never received a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, nursing homes, health insurers, and drug and device manufacturers would gain the most: malpractice payouts for pain and suffering would be capped at $250,000, punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved products would be largely barred, lawyers' fees would be capped, and lawsuits would face shorter deadlines. Providers would also gain a "fair share" rule limiting their liability to their own proportion of fault.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Doctors, insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic (pain-and-suffering) damages at $250,000 per injury, limiting payouts for negligence involving a patient's death, disfigurement, or permanent disability.
Blocks punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products received FDA approval, and prevents prescribing doctors from being named in product liability suits.

Limits lawyer contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% of large recoveries) and lets defendants demand that future damages be paid in installments rather than up front.
Sets a uniform federal deadline for suing — generally one year from discovering an injury and at most three years — shorter than many state deadlines.

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously injured by medical negligence would bear the cost. Someone left severely disabled or disfigured by malpractice could collect no more than $250,000 for pain and suffering beyond actual monetary losses, and families of products that harmed them would have little recourse against FDA-approved drug and device makers. People with the smallest economic losses — children and retirees — would be hit hardest.

drawbacks.text: A flat $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages falls hardest on patients with the smallest measurable economic losses — children, retirees, and stay-at-home parents — since pain, disfigurement, and loss of companionship would be capped at the same fixed figure for everyone.

Manufacturers of FDA-approved drugs and devices would be shielded from punitive damages even when a dangerous product harmed many people, unless the company had hidden required information from the FDA or bribed an official — leaving approval itself as the practical shield.
The shortened one-year-to-discovery, three-year-absolute filing deadline would bar some legitimate claims — including certain childhood injuries — that state law would otherwise allow.
Lawmakers acknowledged an honest cost: federal preemption would override stronger state liability protections that some states had chosen for their own residents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promised lower malpractice premiums and less defensive medicine, but the bulk of its provisions shift the cost of medical mistakes away from providers, insurers, and drug companies and onto injured patients, while overriding state laws that offered fuller compensation. It left actual economic losses recoverable and kept intact a narrow path to punitive damages in cases of outright fraud or bribery of regulators. On balance, the protections for negligent providers and FDA-approved products far outweigh the benefit to patients who were hurt.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and never advanced — no markup on the full bill, no floor vote, nothing in the Senate.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2016, with a single cosponsor, and referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees.
Three days later it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it sat; no further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
The bill never received a floor vote in the House and was never taken up in the Senate, so none of its provisions became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients' current right to sue for medical harm — including full compensation for pain and suffering and punitive damages against negligent drug and device makers — was left untouched, as was the fee system that funds malpractice attorneys.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients' right to sue was preserved

for.name: House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and sent it to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where it was never marked up further or reported

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, with no votes or recorded opposition, so the partisan shape of the fight cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill caps the payouts insurers must make for pain and suffering and limits attorneys' fees, directly shrinking claims costs. Patients who are negligently harmed would bear more of that cost themselves.
Providers gain reduced malpractice exposure, joint-and-several protection, and shorter filing deadlines. Patients injured by negligence would have less recourse and smaller recoveries.
FDA approval would become a near-complete shield against punitive damages, and prescribing doctors could not be named in product suits — a major liability rollback for drug and device companies.
